title: Proposal: Native include attribute for declarative HTML component composition

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### What problem are you trying to solve? Dear Members of the W3C, WHATWG, and the Open Web Community, ​I would like to formally submit a technical proposal aimed at modernizing the core capabilities of HTML to meet the demands of the contemporary web era (2026 and beyond). ​The Problem: Over-Reliance on JavaScript Frameworks for Simple Componentization ​Currently, developers are forced to rely heavily on massive JavaScript runtimes and frameworks (such as React, Vue, or Next.js) just to handle basic tasks like splitting a webpage into reusable components (headers, footers, sidebars). This framework-first approach creates severe bottlenecks: ​Bloated Payload Sizes: Users must download megabytes of JavaScript just to stitch together static pages. ​Performance Hurdles: Low-end mobile devices struggle with heavy client-side JavaScript execution. ​SEO and Hydration Complexity: Pre-rendering fragments requires complex build tools, making the web less accessible to beginner developers. ​The Solution: Native, Attribute-Based Document Composition ​Instead of introducing a brand-new, rigid element like an tag—which can disrupt native DOM semantic structures—I propose introducing a native include attribute that can be attached to any existing block-level or semantic element (e.g.,
,
,
,
,
). ​Proposed HTML6 Syntax Example: ``` Modern Modular Webpage

Loading navigation...

Fetching content, please wait...

``` Why the "Attribute Approach" is Superior to a "New Tag" ​Preserves Semantic Integrity & SEO: By attaching the include feature as an attribute to native semantic elements (like
or
), search engines and screen readers can instantly interpret the structural layout of the page without choking on custom, non-standard elements. ​Layout Predictability & CSS Synergy: Creating a new tag introduces styling ambiguities (e.g., default browser display properties). Applying an attribute to standard tags like
or
means that all modern CSS frameworks, utility classes (e.g., Tailwind), Grid, and Flexbox properties will function seamlessly out of the box. ​Built-in Fallback States: The inner HTML of the host element acts as a native "loading skeleton". If the network fails or is slow, the browser can gracefully display the static placeholder content written inside the tags, drastically improving User Experience (UX). ​Feasibility and Community Alignment ​The massive popularity of declarative libraries like HTMX (using attributes like hx-get) proves that the global developer community is actively looking for a native, HTML-driven approach to modular web building. Standardizing this into the native HTML specification will eliminate third-party dependencies and optimize global data-transfer efficiency. ​Backward Compatibility Guardrail ​To prevent breaking legacy websites, this modern parsing engine could be strictly activated only when the browser detects a specific document type declaration, such as . Older web pages will continue running seamlessly on traditional rendering paths. ​I urge the community and browser engineers to consider this feature for the next iteration of the HTML standard. Let's make the open web fast, semantic, and framework-independent again. ​Thank you for your dedication to the evolution of the World Wide Web. ​Sincerely, [Your GitHub Username / Your Name] On behalf of the Forward-Thinking Open Web Developer Community ### What solutions exist today? _No response_ ### How would you solve it? _No response_ ### Anything else? _No response_
